<h3 align="center">Castaway: one small island, ten hours, and everything starts on the next bar</h3>

<p align="center">
  A stationary-frame lo-fi video for YouTube, in the spirit of the ten-hour streams: one young woman, one tall palm, one raft and a great deal of calm waiting.
  She idles, nodding to the music in her headphones, and every so often something happens: a bottle washes straight back, a shark in headphones nods along,
  a coconut lands on a hermit crab and walks off with the crab wearing it. An unofficial remake inspired by the small-island routines and visual comedy of
  <i>Johnny Castaway</i>, the 1992 desert-island screensaver, in a sunny, hand-painted coastal anime look: 16:9, 1080p, 30 fps, and always daytime.
</p>

<p align="center">
  <b>More than 90 activities</b> on four timers, plus chained follow-ups &middot; every gag starts on the next bar of the music &middot; <b>every sound is synthesized from code</b> &middot; <i>working title, in development</i>
</p>

```sh
python tools/serve.py
# then open http://127.0.0.1:8765/
```

<details>
<summary><b>RELEASE INFO</b>: the four timers, and what a ten-hour run looks like</summary>

```text
              * ZERO KNOTS *  RELEASE INFO  * ZERO KNOTS *
              - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -

  TITLE ............................................. CASTAWAY (working)
  TYPE ....................... stationary-frame lo-fi island video, 16:9
  LENGTH ........................................... 10:00:00, seed 1992
  PICTURE ......................................... 1080p, 30 fps, sunny
  BARS ..................................... 12,000, one every 3 seconds
  NIGHT SCENES ....................................................... 0

  TIMER ....... COMES ROUND ................... IN A TYPICAL 10-HOUR RUN
  regular ..... every 2 to 5 minutes ......................... about 155
  occasional .. every 12 to 25 minutes ........................ about 30
  rare ........ every 30 to 60 minutes ........................ about 13
  super rare .. every 3 to 6 hours .......... about 2, never more than 3
  follow-ups .. chained to something else ..................... about 20
  idle ........ the rest of the time ............ about two thirds of it
```

The counts are the median of 200 simulated runs, as the header of [activities.toml](activities.toml) says. When a timer goes off it picks one activity from its tier, by weight, among the ones free to run. Lanes let things overlap, so a ship can sail past while she is busy with a coconut; the ship will even wait up to ten minutes for her to get busy. Every activity starts on the next bar of the music, every 3 seconds, so every punchline lands on the beat. `python tools/schedule.py` checks the file and simulates a ten-hour run, and `python tools/render_demo.py --dev` renders a dev reel of every activity with a heads-up display (the older Python reference renderer).

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>THE SOUND AND THE MACHINERY</b></summary>

- **Sound.** Every sound is synthesized from code by [tools/make_audio.py](tools/make_audio.py): no samples, stock loops or recordings, so no third-party licence applies. More than 150 sound files so far. The theme is a seamless 60-second loop at 80 BPM in F major (a ii-V-I-vi progression), 20 bars of exactly 3 seconds, with electric piano, a kalimba lead, soft drums and vinyl crackle. The ocean ambience is a seamless 60-second loop too. The mix sits at -14 LUFS with true peak at or below -1 dBTP, and levels are adjustable in master and per routine. Nobody has listened to it yet: so far it has only been measured.
- **Picture.** Sunny, hand-painted coastal anime, 16:9, rendered at 1080p and 30 fps, always daytime. Hard cuts and stepped movement are the motion defaults (the cogs above agree). Scene life has 26 entries: shore waves and drifting cloud shadows are built; distant birds, planes with vapour trails, whale pods, dolphins, sailboats, sandpipers, a gecko and a rain shower are planned.
- **Renderer.** A web page ([web/index.html](web/index.html)) with live preview and export. It encodes frame-exact H.264 in the browser with WebCodecs (68 to 78 frames a second at 1080p30 in Chrome), and the server mixes the sound and joins the two into a YouTube-ready MP4. Plain ES modules, no build step, no npm packages.
- **Status.** In development. No video has been published yet, so for now the only way to watch is to run it.

</details>

<h1 align="center">CASTAWAY</h1>

<p align="center">
  <b>Ten hours of one tiny island. Almost nothing happens, on purpose.</b><br>
  She idles. Every so often, something happens. In between, a cloud shadow drifts over.
</p>

Castaway (working title) is a stationary-frame lo-fi video for YouTube, in the spirit of the ten-hour lofi streams: a young woman alone on a tiny island with one tall palm, a raft and a lot of time. She mostly idles, nodding to the music on her headphones, and every so often something happens. A message in a bottle washes up and washes straight back out. A coconut falls on a hermit crab, and the coconut walks off with the crab wearing it. A shark in headphones nods along to the beat. It is an unofficial remake inspired by the small-island routines and visual comedy of *Johnny Castaway*, the 1992 desert-island screensaver, repainted as a sunny, hand-painted coastal anime scene. 16:9, 1080p, 30 fps, and always daytime.

The gags live in [activities.toml](activities.toml): more than 90 activities, most of them on four timers, from everyday routines every 2 to 5 minutes to super-rare callbacks every 3 to 6 hours, and each one waits for the next bar of the music (3 seconds) so the gags land on the beat. Every sound is synthesized from code by [tools/make_audio.py](tools/make_audio.py): no samples, no recordings, no borrowed loops, so no third-party licence.

```sh
python tools/serve.py
# then open http://127.0.0.1:8765/
```

<p align="center">
  <sub>Live preview in the browser, then export a frame-exact, YouTube-ready MP4. Plain ES modules, no build step, no npm.<br>
  In development: no video has been published yet, so for now the only way to watch her wait is to run it.</sub>
</p>

<details>
<summary><b>THE TIDE TABLE</b>: how the banner moves without moving anything</summary>

```text
 THE TIDE TABLE · ONE PALETTE PERIOD · 12 SECONDS · 85 STEPS
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
         index 0                                                 index 84
   0 s  │          ░░░░▒▒▒▒▓▓▓▓▓███████████████████▓▓▓▓▓▒▒▒░░░░░         │
   3 s  │▒▒▓▓▓▓▓███████████████████▓▓▓▓▓▒▒▒▒░░░░                   ░░░░▒▒│
   6 s  │██████████▓▓▓▓▒▒▒▒░░░░░                  ░░░░░▒▒▒▒▓▓▓▓██████████│
   9 s  │▒▒░░░░░                   ░░░░▒▒▒▒▓▓▓▓████████████████████▓▓▓▓▒▒│
  12 s  │          ░░░░▒▒▒▒▓▓▓▓▓███████████████████▓▓▓▓▓▒▒▒░░░░░         │
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  The picture is a grid of numbers, worked out once and never touched
  again. The only thing that moves is this row: the colour ring, slowly
  turning. At 12 s the tide is back where it started and the name is
  still there. The video runs on roughly the same plan, for ten hours,
  with something small happening every 2 to 5 minutes.
```

**How the banner works.** The plasma is a sum of five sines, computed once by the banner's generator into a 320 by 90 index image (85 steps to a palette period) and embedded as a small greyscale PNG drawn with square VGA pixels. The colour comes from an SVG filter doing the old 256-colour trick: one stage adds an offset to every index, animated across one whole period every 12 seconds (four bars of the theme), and the next looks the result up in a colour table that repeats. Nothing is redrawn; the bands crawl because the table turns.

**The name is pressed in, not painted on.** Inside the letters the index image holds a second copy of the plasma, half a period out of phase and nudged a few pixels down and to the right, read through the same ramp lifted towards the pale end. So CASTAWAY is a raised, lighter patch of the same field, and its bands jump at every edge. A static layer adds the one-pixel highlight on the lit side and the shadow on the other. The heavy Roman capitals were drawn for this banner from polygons, ellipses and one broad-nib pen stroke (the S), then leaned back through a perspective transform and rasterised with 4 x 4 supersampling.

**The roll.** One of the mid-90s intros this look comes from picked its colour scheme at random every time it started. This one rolls at build time instead, from a seeded generator: seed 1992, the same seed as the video's default run, came up lagoon. The generator takes `--roll=crimson` (or green, coral, sun, violet) if you would rather have a different sea.

**The clock.** Ten pages of text, six seconds each, so the banner loops every 60 seconds, the same length as the theme: twenty bars, five turns of the tide, eighty nods. With reduced motion switched on, the palette stops, the first page stays put and she stops nodding. She does not seem to mind.

The style is credited to Razor 1911's DOS intros #02 and #03 (code by Hetero, December 1996 and January 1997), where a one-hue plasma fills the screen and the group's name shows only as a displacement in it. Nothing of theirs is copied here: no letters, no sprites, no palette, no words.

</details>

Every activity starts on the next bar of the music, so the gags land on the beat. Every sound is synthesized from code by [tools/make_audio.py](tools/make_audio.py).

<details>
<summary><b>CASTAWAY.NFO</b>: the timetable, the gags and the greetings, the way a loader would have shipped them</summary>

```text

║                    I D L E   H A N D S   P R E S E N T S                   ║
║                                                                            ║
║         C A S T A W A Y   ·   a ten-hour lo-fi island, on purpose          ║
╠════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  WHAT ...... one tiny island, one tall palm, one raft, one young woman     ║
║              in cream headphones, and a lot of time                        ║
║  FORMAT .... 16:9 · 1080p · 24 fps · always daytime                        ║
║  RUN ....... 10:00:00 · seed 1992 · same seed, same video                  ║
```

The counts are the median of 200 simulated ten-hour runs, as the header of [activities.toml](activities.toml) says, and the activity count was 94 on 2026-10-01: 81 on the four timers and 13 chained follow-ups (it grows every few hours). Lanes let things overlap, so a ship can sail past while she is busy with a coconut, and she is busy about a third of the time. Super-rare events are capped at three a run. `python tools/schedule.py` checks the file and simulates a run; the default is 10:00:00 with seed 1992, and the same seed makes the same video, event for event.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>THE MACHINERY</b>: the sound, the renderer and the tools</summary>

**The sound.** Everything is synthesized by [tools/make_audio.py](tools/make_audio.py): no samples, loops or recordings, so no third-party licence applies. More than 150 sound files so far (181 on 2026-10-01). The theme is a seamless 60-second loop at 80 BPM in F major, a ii-V-I-vi progression over 20 bars of exactly 3 seconds, with electric piano, a kalimba lead, soft drums and vinyl crackle. The ocean ambience is another seamless 60-second loop. The mix sits at -14 LUFS with true peak at or below -1 dBTP, and the levels are adjustable for the master and per routine. It has been measured with great care and listened to by nobody, so this page will not tell you how it sounds. The loader above is silent, which seemed only fair.

**The picture.** The renderer is a web page, [web/index.html](web/index.html), served by [tools/serve.py](tools/serve.py): live preview, then a frame-exact export in the browser (WebCodecs H.264; in Chrome it measured 68 to 78 frames a second at 1080p30), after which the server mixes the sound and joins the two into an MP4. Hard cuts and stepped movement are the motion defaults. Around her, the scene has 26 entries of its own (4 always-on effects, 22 timed events): shore waves and drifting cloud shadows are built; distant birds, planes with vapour trails, whale pods, dolphins, sailboats, sandpipers, a gecko and a rain shower are planned.

**The tools.**

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `python tools/serve.py` | serves the renderer at http://127.0.0.1:8765/ and mixes the export |
| `python tools/schedule.py` | validates [activities.toml](activities.toml) and simulates a ten-hour run |
| `python tools/render_demo.py --dev` | the older Python reference renderer: a dev reel of every activity with a heads-up display |
| `python tools/make_audio.py` | synthesizes every sound |

The working log, with every decision and what is still open, is [MUSING.md](MUSING.md).

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>HOW THE LOADER WORKS</b>: palette rotation, a hammock made of a subtitle, and a scroll that steps</summary>

The banner borrows the look of the first graphical PC intros, from 1990 to 1993, when VGA mode 13h gave you 320 by 200 pixels and 256 colours picked from a palette: a framed metal plate, gradient bars, small magenta capitals on an arc, and one big scroller. It is drawn on that same 320-pixel-wide grid, and every colour is snapped to the VGA's 6 bits per channel, so the ramps band the way the real ones did.

**Palette rotation.** The diamonds behind the plate never move. Each ring is one of 16 palette entries, and the palette turns one step every sixteenth of a bar, so a band of light seems to travel outward while every pixel stays where it is. One turn takes 3 seconds, one bar of the theme. It is a stationary frame in which things appear to happen, which is the whole video in a 32-pixel tile.

**The hammock.** In the period loaders, an arc like this under the logo carried the group's full name. Here it carries the pitch, EVERY SO OFTEN, SOMETHING HAPPENS, hung from two rings under the plate, and she lies in it. Nothing else happens to her in the banner. She lifts her head on every beat and taps a foot, which is a fair summary of the other two thirds of the video. (The hammock is also a real activity in the schedule, on the rare timer. There, she ties one end to the palm, looks round for a second tree, finds none, and ties the other end to the raft. A metal plate is, if anything, an upgrade.)

**The choppy scroll.** Period scrollers stepped a few pixels at a time, and people noticed. This one moves exactly 4 pixels per step, 16 steps a second, which is also Castaway's own house rule: hard cuts and stepped movement. The text is followed by a copy of its own beginning, so the lap of about five minutes wraps without a seam. Everything else loops on the beat: the bars swing once every two bars of the theme, the glints wink every two bars, and the head and the foot go once a beat. With reduced motion switched on, it all holds still on the first frame, which already says CASTAWAY twice.

**Credits.** The style is modelled on early PC loaders by The Humble Guys, INC, USA and Fairlight, TRSI with The Dream Team, and Razor 1911 with Skillion. They are credited here as the reference only: none of their logos, letterforms or names appear in the banner, and IDLE HANDS is invented. The banner is an SVG built by a dependency-free Node script, with no text elements, no filters and no scripts.

</details>

<br>

<h1 align="center">Castaway</h1>

<p align="center">
  <b>A ten-hour lo-fi island video. Estimated time remaining: 10:00:00.</b><br>
  <sub><i>Working title. In development. The ETA is not a bug, it is the product.</i></sub>
</p>

One tiny island, one tall palm, one raft and one young woman in headphones. She mostly idles, nodding to the music, and every so often something happens: a message in a bottle washes straight back, a coconut lands on a hermit crab who walks off wearing it, a shark in headphones nods along, a ship sails past exactly while she is busy. A stationary-frame video for YouTube in the spirit of the ten-hour lo-fi streams, and an unofficial remake inspired by the small-island routines and visual comedy of *Johnny Castaway*, the 1992 desert-island screensaver, reimagined as a sunny coastal anime scene with a hand-painted look. 16:9, 1080p, always daytime.

There are more than 90 activities, most of them on four timers that go off every 2 to 5 minutes at the busy end and every 3 to 6 hours at the other. Each one starts on the next bar of the music, so the gags land on the beat. Every sound is synthesized from code. Nothing is sampled.

```sh
python tools/serve.py
# then open http://127.0.0.1:8765/
```

That is the whole install: a web page with a live preview of the island and an export to a YouTube-ready MP4. No setup wizard, no build step, no npm packages. Click INSTALL once; the waiting takes care of itself.

<h1 align="center">Castaway <sup>+10</sup></h1>

<p align="center">
  <b>A ten-hour lo-fi island video with ten options. All ten are locked, on purpose.</b><br>
  <sub>working title · in development, nothing published yet · an unofficial remake inspired by the 1992 screensaver <i>Johnny Castaway</i></sub>
</p>

**Castaway** is a stationary-frame lo-fi video for YouTube, in the spirit of the ten-hour streams: a young woman alone on a tiny island with one tall palm, a raft and a lot of time. She mostly idles, nodding to the music in her headphones, and every so often, always on the next bar of the music, something happens. A bottle she throws washes straight back. A drone delivers a parcel, and the parcel is more headphones. A shark surfaces in headphones and nods along. Sunny, hand-painted coastal anime, 16:9 at 1080p, and always daytime.

Four timers and more than 90 activities decide what happens and when, and every sound in it is synthesized from code: no samples, no borrowed loops, no recordings. The menu up there cannot change any of that. Nobody can. It is a feature.

```sh
python tools/serve.py
# then open http://127.0.0.1:8765/
```

<sub>Live preview, and export to a YouTube-ready MP4: the browser encodes frame-exact H.264 and the server mixes in the sound. Plain ES modules, no build step, no npm packages.</sub>

<pre>
            ATOLL ORDER presents CASTAWAY +7: the keys that do work

  F1  <a href="tools/serve.py">START THE ISLAND</a> ............................... python tools/serve.py
  F2  <a href="web/index.html">WATCH LIVE, EXPORT THE MP4</a> .................... http://127.0.0.1:8765/
  F3  <a href="tools/schedule.py">SIMULATE TEN HOURS OF IT</a> .................... python tools/schedule.py
  F4  <a href="tools/make_audio.py">SYNTHESIZE EVERY SOUND</a> .................... python tools/make_audio.py
  F5  <a href="tools/render_demo.py">DEV REEL, ONE OF EVERYTHING</a> ........ python tools/render_demo.py --dev
  F6  <a href="activities.toml">READ THE TIMERS</a> ...................................... activities.toml
  F7  <a href="MUSING.md">READ THE LOG</a> ............................................... MUSING.md

  ENTER: F1, then F2.     ESC: see F9 in the picture.     F8 to F10: locked.
</pre>

<details>
<summary><b>OPTIONS.TXT</b>: why all ten options are locked</summary>

<br>

| Key | Option | State | Why it will not budge |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| F1 | Unlimited daylight | `ON` | Always daytime. It is a project rule, not a setting: no night scenes, ever. |
| F2 | Something happens | `SOON-ISH` | Four timers: regular every 2 to 5 minutes, occasional every 12 to 25, rare every 30 to 60, super rare every 3 to 6 hours (three at most per run). |
| F3 | Ship stops for her | `OFF` | Lanes let things overlap, so a ship can cross the horizon while she is busy with a coconut. It even waits for her to get busy. Headphones. It sails on. In a super-rare one she spots a ship and waves like mad, and it sounds its horn back. Then it sails on. |
| F4 | Samples or recordings | `NONE` | More than 150 sound files, every one synthesized from code by [tools/make_audio.py](tools/make_audio.py): no samples, no borrowed loops, no recordings, so no third-party licence. |
| F5 | Gags land on the beat | `ON` | Every activity starts on the next bar of the music, and a bar is exactly 3 seconds. |
| F6 | Phone signal | `1 BAR` | The signal hunt ends at the very top of the palm, with one bar. |
| F7 | Headphone delivery | `BY DRONE` | A drone lowers a parcel. Inside: another pair of headphones. Later a wave lifts the empty box and floats it off to sea. |
| F8 | Bottle stays away | `OFF` | Her message in a bottle washes straight back. Much later, a different bottle brings a reply. |
| F9 | Leave the island | `ANY TIME` | Super rare: she stands, stretches and walks off over the water. The island sits empty for twenty seconds. She comes back with an iced coffee. Never explained. |
| F10 | Random seed | `1992` | The default run is 10:00:00 on seed 1992: same seed, same ten hours, bar for bar. |

In the banner the cursor rests on each option for two bars (6 seconds), so it goes round all ten once per loop of the 60-second theme. The key goes down on beat three, the state flips for one beat, and it flips back. F9 is the exception: it holds while she is gone.

</details>

<h3 align="center">CASTAWAY <sub><i>(working title)</i></sub></h3>

<p align="center">
  <b>A ten-hour lo-fi island video in which almost nothing happens, on purpose.</b><br>
  She idles. Every so often, something happens. The camera never moves, so all the spinning went up there.
</p>

A stationary-frame lo-fi video for YouTube, in the spirit of the ten-hour lofi streams: a young woman alone on a tiny island with one tall palm, a raft and a lot of time. She mostly idles, nodding to the music on her headphones, and every so often something happens. A message in a bottle washes straight back. A delivery drone drops a parcel, and the parcel is another pair of headphones. A shark in headphones nods along to the beat. It is an unofficial remake inspired by the small-island routines and visual comedy of *Johnny Castaway*, the 1992 desert-island screensaver, repainted as a sunny, hand-painted coastal anime scene: 16:9, 1080p, 30 fps, and always daytime.

The gags live in [activities.toml](activities.toml): more than 90 of them, most on four timers and the rest chained to something else. Something regular every 2 to 5 minutes, occasional every 12 to 25, rare every 30 to 60, super rare every 3 to 6 hours. A typical ten-hour run comes to about 155 regular, 30 occasional, 13 rare and 2 super-rare events, plus chained follow-ups, and she is busy about a third of the time. Every activity waits for the next bar of the music, so the gags land on the beat. Every sound is synthesized from code by [tools/make_audio.py](tools/make_audio.py): no samples, loops or recordings, so no third-party licence applies. It is loudness-checked, peak-limited, and so far unheard by anyone.

```sh
python tools/serve.py
# then open http://127.0.0.1:8765/
```

Live preview in the page, then export a YouTube-ready MP4: the browser encodes frame-exact H.264 (WebCodecs) and the server mixes in the sound. Plain ES modules, no build step, no npm. In development: nothing is published yet, so to watch her do nothing for ten hours you will have to run it yourself.

Six white wireframes turning slowly on dashed turntables, labelled in sand-coloured capitals: BOTTLE (eight-sided, corked, a rolled message inside), CRATE (boarded sides), PARCEL (tied with string and a bow), HEADPHONES (two cups and a padded band), ICED COFFEE (tapered cup, domed lid, straw) and SANDCASTLE (a keep with battlements and a flag).">
</p>

- **Bottle.** Thrown out to sea, it washes straight back. A different bottle, much later, brings a reply.
- **Crate.** A stray cat (grey tabby, white chest) arrives on one, climbs the palm and naps. One day it floats away again. Another day it comes back.
- **Parcel.** Delivered by drone. Contents: headphones.
- **Headphones.** The spare pair. See parcel.
- **Iced coffee.** She could leave any time. Once in a long while she walks out over the water and comes back with one.
- **Sandcastle.** She builds it. The tide takes it: the tide is a chained follow-up, and it comes for the castle 5 to 30 minutes later.

The video has no turntables: hard cuts and stepped movement are the project's motion defaults. The spinning is a README privilege.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>OBJECT FILE 01</b>: how the banner works</summary>

```text
 ROCKPOOL POLYGON SOCIETY · OBJECT FILE 01 · "A COCONUT, ROUGHLY"
 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  shape ......... a cube with a low pyramid on every face
  faces ......... 24 triangles, two-tone like a chessboard
  vertices ...... 14
  glass ......... white at 46 percent, coral pink at 74 percent
  motion ........ two turns about y and one about x every 30 s, plus a
                  slow sway about z
  frames ........ 48 per 30 s; the browser fills in the rest
  depth sort .... none: every face is see-through, so nobody can tell
  nods .......... once a beat, 4 px down, 80 times a minute
  resemblance ... to a coconut: some
 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

**The glenz.** The generator rotates the object on three axes, projects it with perspective and writes every face as one SVG polygon whose corners and colour are lists of 48 keyframes, one 30-second cycle's worth. Faces are lit by their angle to a light in the top left, so they change tint as they turn, and they are drawn see-through, so the back of the object shows through the front and overlaps come out brighter. That is the glenz look, and the reason it never needed a depth sort.

**The dot scroller.** Forty character slots sit on a ring round the object's middle, tilted towards you. They all share one animation (a full turn: position on the ellipse, squash, slope and brightness) and differ only in where they start. The ring is drawn twice, the far half behind the glass and the near half in front. Each slot holds four letters and swaps to the next one while it is directly behind the object, so 40 slots carry up to 160 characters, one turn every 15 seconds.

**The vector balls.** CASTAWAY is 120 shaded balls in a 5 by 7 grid per letter, floating on a slow wave. Once a minute, on bar 4, the letters flip right round one after another, half a beat apart. Every ball knows its distance from its letter's axis and feeds it to one shared animation, which swings it round and scales it for depth. Every so often something happens: the banner does it too.

**The rest.** A text writer types five pages with hard cuts between them. A ripple leaves the object on every bar and spreads for four. Every period divides 60 seconds, the length of the theme (20 bars of 3 seconds at 80 BPM), so the whole banner loops when the music would. No script, no fonts, no filters, no GIF: shapes, CSS and SMIL. With reduced motion switched on it holds still on a complete first frame.

</details>

Castaway is an unofficial project inspired by *Johnny Castaway* (1992), which belongs to its owners; nothing from it is used here. The Rockpool Polygon Society and everyone in the greetz are made up. Glenz, dot scrollers, vector balls and wireframes are demoscene staples, credited here as a genre; the object, the fonts, the props and the copy were built from scratch by the generator.

More: [MUSING.md](MUSING.md) (the project log), [web/index.html](web/index.html) (the renderer page), [tools/schedule.py](tools/schedule.py), [tools/render_demo.py](tools/render_demo.py).

<details>
<summary><b>TUNNEL NOTES</b>: one ring per beat, and why the island never gets any closer</summary>

```text
 LOOKUP LAGOON · TUNNEL NOTES                           ONE RING PER BEAT
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 RINGS ............. 16 in flight, each a band of 32 checkered cells
 SPAWN ............. one new ring per beat: 80 BPM, 0.75 s, the tempo
                     of the theme
 SPEED ............. the walls double in size every bar (3 s)
 TWIST ............. each ring sits half a cell round from the last
 ROLL .............. 10 degrees a second. the far end circles once
                     every 36 s, which counts as excitement round here
 THE FAR END ....... a tiny island in daylight, kept the right way up.
                     she nods on every beat. it never gets any closer
 SIGNS ............. one gag flies out of the island every bar and
                     swerves past you on the way out:
                     coconut, bottle (again), sea turtle, more
                     headphones, cat on a crate, one bar of signal,
                     shark (nodding), sandcastle, the tide, a hydrofoil
                     shaka, iced coffee, kumara
 THE COCONUT ....... the one on top of the logo has a hermit crab in
                     it. it walks C-A-S-T-A and back in eighth notes
 ETA ............... 10:00:00. it does not count down. it never will
 LOOP .............. 36 s (12 bars), then exactly the same again
 REDUCED MOTION .... everything holds still on the first frame. so
                     does she, mostly
```

The banner is the trailer. In the video, the busiest timer goes off every 2 to 5 minutes, and she spends about two thirds of the run doing nothing in particular, beautifully. The signs above are roughly half an hour of her day, delivered in 36 seconds.

The other effect, the spinning sand tiles round the run command, is a rotozoomer: one small tile repeated to infinity, turned and zoomed about the middle. Both effects move the texture and leave the subject alone, which is also how Castaway treats its castaway.

</details>

[activities.toml](activities.toml) held 94 activities on 2026-10-01 (81 on the four timers, 13 chained follow-ups), and more arrive every few hours. Lanes let things overlap: she has one, and the cat, the turtle, the sea and sky, and the shore each have their own, so a ship can sail past while she is busy with a coconut. The ship has a lane and a sense of timing. She has headphones.

The scene has a life of its own too: 26 entries, 4 always-on effects and 22 timed events. Shore waves and drifting cloud shadows are built; distant birds, planes with vapour trails, whale pods, dolphins, sailboats, sandpipers, a gecko and a rain shower are planned. Run `python tools/schedule.py` to check the schedule and simulate a ten-hour run.

<br>

| Greeted | Why |

Between visitors she keeps herself busy: coconut sipping, fishing, jogging laps, a sandcastle that the tide takes, waving for rescue, the signal hunt (one bar of signal, at the top of the palm), and bushcraft: fire by friction, a hammock, a lookout up the palm, spear fishing. She could leave any time: she walks out over the water and comes back with an iced coffee.

<details>
<summary><b>THE SCHEDULE</b>: four timers and a great deal of calm</summary>

<br>

[activities.toml](activities.toml) listed 94 activities on 2026-10-01 (81 on four timers, 13 chained follow-ups that only start when another activity calls them), and it grows every few hours. In a typical 10-hour run (the median of 200 simulated runs):

| Timer | Comes round every | Events in a 10-hour run |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Regular | 2 to 5 minutes | about 155 |
| Occasional | 12 to 25 minutes | about 30 |
| Rare | 30 to 60 minutes | about 13 |
| Super rare | 3 to 6 hours (at most 3 a run) | about 2 |

Plus chained follow-ups, such as the tide that comes for each sandcastle. She is busy about a third of the time and idles the rest. Lanes let things overlap, so a ship can sail past while she is busy with a coconut. Every activity starts on the next bar of the music, every 3 seconds. The default run is 10:00:00 with seed 1992.

The scene has a life of its own too: 26 entries, 4 always-on effects and 22 timed events. Shore waves and drifting cloud shadows are built; distant birds, planes with vapour trails, whale pods, dolphins, sailboats, sandpipers, a gecko and a rain shower are planned.

```sh

python tools/render_demo.py --dev  # dev reel of every activity, with a HUD
```

<br>

- Everything is synthesized from code in [tools/make_audio.py](tools/make_audio.py): no samples, borrowed loops or recordings, so no third-party licence applies. More than 150 sound files so far.
- The theme is a seamless 60-second loop at 80 BPM in F major (a ii-V-I-vi progression): 20 bars of exactly 3 seconds, with electric piano, a kalimba lead, soft drums and vinyl crackle. The ocean ambience is a seamless 60-second loop as well.

<br>


<details>
<summary><b>ABOUT THIS INTRO</b>: how the banner is made</summary>

<br>

The banner copies the layout of a mid-1980s Commodore 64 one-screen intro, the kind that ran before the main program: a big logo on black, a fenced PRESENTS, one line on a pink raster bar and one on a blue one, a dated "... ON dd/mm/yy BY ..." line, a small info block, a blinking PRESS SPACE and one scroller. Here the date line says who stranded her (the random seed), and the info block lists the plot.

- **Logo.** A character mosaic: each letter is 4 or 5 cells wide and 6 high, every cell full, empty, a half block or a 45-degree wedge. It clips a stack of one-scanline stripes (a sea ramp, then a sand ramp) that rolls up 16 lines a second, which is the raster split, rolling.
- **Colours.** Only the 16 VIC-II colours, at Pepto's measured values. Bar shading and fades run in luminance order.
- **Type.** An 8x8 font drawn for this banner; the scroller is the same font at 2x2, shaded per scanline.
- **Sprites.** Two 24x21 sprites, expanded to double size. A real C64 would need more sprites than it owns to colour them like this, so consider them aspirational.
- **Motion.** Everything but the scroller keeps time with the theme at 80 BPM: the sprites nod and PRESS SPACE blinks on the beat, a glint runs down each bar once a beat, the colour wash goes round once a beat and the logo stripes come round every two. No colour cycle brings white back to the same spot more than 1.4 times a second, well under the 3 Hz flash limit, and with reduced motion switched on everything holds on a complete first frame.

No group's logo, character set, picture or scrolltext was copied; every letter, sprite and word is new, and the whole banner is rebuilt by one small Node script with no dependencies.

</details>

<h3 align="center">CASTAWAY <sub><i>(working title)</i></sub></h3>

<p align="center">
  <b>Ten hours on one very small island. She stays. Everything else drifts by.</b><br>
  She idles, nodding to the music on her headphones. Every so often something happens, and quite often it arrives by sea.
</p>

<p align="center">
  <kbd>DYCP</kbd> every character at its own height
  &nbsp;·&nbsp;
  <kbd>HER</kbd> sand level, mostly
  &nbsp;·&nbsp;
  <kbd>SAMPLES</kbd> 0
</p>

**Castaway** is a stationary-frame lo-fi video for YouTube, in the spirit of the ten-hour lofi streams: a young woman alone on a tiny island with one tall palm, a raft and a lot of time. She mostly idles. Every so often, a message in a bottle washes straight back, a stray cat arrives on a crate and naps up the palm, or a shark in headphones surfaces and nods to the beat. It is an unofficial remake inspired by the small-island routines and visual comedy of *Johnny Castaway*, the 1992 desert-island screensaver, repainted in a sunny, hand-painted coastal anime style: 16:9, 1080p, 24 fps, and always daytime.

[activities.toml](activities.toml) holds more than 90 activities on four timers (plus the follow-ups they set off), from a coconut every few minutes to "she could leave any time" once in a very long while. Every one of them starts on the next bar of the music, so the gags land on the beat. Every sound is synthesized from code by [tools/make_audio.py](tools/make_audio.py): no samples, no borrowed loops, no recordings.

```sh
python tools/serve.py
# then open http://127.0.0.1:8765/
```

The page plays a live preview and exports a YouTube-ready MP4. In development: no video has been published yet, so for now the only way to watch her wait is to run it.

A different bottle brings a reply to hers, hours later. The cat comes back another time. The scroller has no room for that much patience; she has plenty.

<details>
<summary><b>HOW THE BANNER WORKS</b>: DYCP, FLD, tech-tech, and one sine table</summary>

**DYCP** is Different Y Character Position: the Commodore 64 scroller in which every character of the line sits at its own height, so the text ripples along a sine as it scrolls. Here every letter and sprite is a reference to one shared glyph, and all of them run the same stepped sine track (whole-pixel steps, like a table in memory), each with its own delay, while the whole line slides left. The wave is about 256 pixels long and drifts slowly right, against the text. The letters sit in a mask over fixed bands of colour, so each one turns yellow on a crest, green on the way down and blue in a trough, the way a raster colour split would do it.

**FLD** pushed whole rows of a screen up and down; here the CAST row hops on the first beat of every bar and AWAY a beat later. **Tech-tech** slid each scanline of a logo sideways; here it is the wave lines of the sea under the island, each one a little behind the line above. The logo letters are fat squared capitals sampled on the multicolour grid (pixels twice as wide as they are tall), filled with a diagonal stripe pattern that cycles one pixel at a time. Every colour on the screen is one of the C64's sixteen, except her skin tone; even the logo's drop shadow is just the next darker colour of each panel stripe.

The look is the C64 DYCP demo part of 1989 to 1992. The references are Sphinx's *DYCP Mania* (1989), for the striped logo on mauve panels, and The Force's *DYCP Intro* (1991), for the scroller hanging under a two-row logo. They are credited here as the reference; none of their logos, charsets or pictures were copied, and everything in the banner was drawn from scratch by its generator. No script, no GIF, no filters, and with reduced motion switched on, the whole screen holds still on its first frame.

</details>

<p align="center">
  <b>A ten-hour lo-fi island video in which almost nothing happens, on purpose.</b><br>
  One young woman in cream headphones, one tall palm, one raft and a great deal of very calm waiting.
  She idles. Every so often, something happens. Today it happened to a crab.<br>
  <sub>Working title, in development. 16:9, 1080p, 30 fps, always daytime. An unofficial remake inspired by the small-island routines and visual comedy of the 1992 screensaver <i>Johnny Castaway</i>.</sub>
</p>

From the project root. No build step and no npm packages, just plain ES modules and a small Python server:

```sh
python tools/serve.py        # then open http://127.0.0.1:8765/
python tools/schedule.py     # check the schedule, simulate a 10-hour run
```

The page plays a live preview and exports a YouTube-ready MP4: the browser encodes every frame exactly with WebCodecs (H.264, 68 to 78 frames a second at 1080p30 in Chrome), and the server mixes the sound and joins the two with ffmpeg.

<details>
<summary><b>What happens, and how often</b>: four timers, and every gag lands on the bar</summary>
<br>

Everything she can do lives in [activities.toml](activities.toml): more than 90 activities as of October 2026, each with its own step-by-step beats, how long it lasts and how often it comes round. Most sit on four timers; a dozen or so only ever follow on from something else. Typical counts are the median of 200 simulated 10-hour runs, as the file's own header gives them:

```text
TIMER        COMES ROUND EVERY     IN 10 HOURS
-----------  --------------------  -----------
REGULAR      2 TO 5 MINUTES               ~155
OCCASIONAL   12 TO 25 MINUTES              ~30
RARE         30 TO 60 MINUTES              ~13
SUPER RARE   3 TO 6 HOURS (MAX 3)           ~2
CHAINED      AFTER SOMETHING ELSE          ~20
```

She is busy about a third of the time and idling the rest. Every activity starts on the next bar of the music, every 3 seconds, so the gags land on the beat. Lanes let things overlap, so the world can carry on while she is busy. The default run is `10:00:00` with seed `1992`, and the same seed always gives the same schedule.

Things that may happen while you are looking the other way:

- A coconut falls on a hermit crab. Then the coconut walks off, with the crab wearing it.
- A message in a bottle washes straight back to her feet. Much later, a different bottle brings a reply.
- A delivery drone arrives. The parcel is another pair of headphones.
- A sea turtle visits.
- A stray grey tabby with a white chest arrives on a crate, climbs the palm and naps. One day it floats away again. It comes back another time.
- The signal hunt: one bar, at the top of the palm.
- A shark in headphones surfaces and nods along to the beat.
- A tour boat full of selfie-takers.
- She could leave any time: she walks out over the water and comes back with an iced coffee.
- A bro on an electric hydrofoil waves a shaka and carves off.
- Bushcraft: fire by friction, a hammock, a lookout up the palm, spear fishing.
- A kumara, planted, that grows over the course of the video.
- And the regulars: coconut sipping, fishing, jogging laps, waving for rescue, and a sandcastle that stands until the tide takes it.

The scene keeps itself busy too: 26 bits of scene life, 4 always on and 22 timed. Shore waves and drifting cloud shadows are built; distant birds, planes with vapour trails, whale pods, dolphins, sailboats, sandpipers, a gecko and a rain shower are planned.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>The sound</b>: every note is made from code</summary>
<br>

Every sound is synthesized by [tools/make_audio.py](tools/make_audio.py): more than 150 files, none of them sampled, recorded or lifted from a loop pack, so no third-party licence applies. The theme is a seamless 60-second loop at 80 BPM in F major (ii, V, I, vi), 20 bars of exactly 3 seconds, with electric piano, a kalimba lead, soft drums and vinyl crackle. The ocean ambience is a seamless 60-second loop too. The mix sits at -14 LUFS with true peak at or below -1 dBTP, and the levels can be set for the master and for each routine.

Nobody has listened to any of it yet. The waveforms look extremely relaxed.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>How the picture is drawn</b>: 1000 cells and one background colour</summary>
<br>

It is a PETSCII picture: a Commodore 64 text screen, 40 cells across and 25 down, and every cell holds one 8 by 8 character from the machine's own set of blocks, wedges, lines, arcs and capitals, or its reverse. The rules are the machine's: one background colour for the whole picture, and one colour per cell on top of it. The generator keeps them; a cell cannot hold two foreground colours even by accident.

```basic
10 POKE 53280,14 : REM BORDER: LIGHT BLUE
20 POKE 53281,3  : REM BACKGROUND: CYAN. THE SKY. THERE IS ONLY ONE.
30 REM COLOUR 0 IS BLACK. IT IS IN NONE OF THE 1000 CELLS.
40 REM IT IS ALWAYS DAYTIME.
```

The background is cyan, so the sky comes free and everything else is built a cell at a time. That is why the palm's fronds bend in 45-degree steps and the island ends in wedges. Where the sand meets the sea a cell would need yellow and blue at once, which it cannot have, so it shows yellow and cyan instead, and the cyan becomes shallow water. That is a colour clash. Here it is the scenery.

The title is typed in reverse video in blue, so its letters are the background showing through: CASTAWAY is written in the sky, under the sea.

It moves the only way PETSCII moves, by changing characters, and only on the music's grid: 80 BPM, a beat every 0.75 seconds, a bar every 3. The loop is 20 bars, 60 seconds, the length of the theme. Brackets of sound pulse beside her headphones on every beat, the foam swaps every half bar, the sun swaps its rays every bar, the caption changes every two, a glint crosses the title every four, and the coconut lands exactly on a bar line, 18 seconds in. From 40.5 seconds a sea turtle swims into the shallows a cell per beat, naps, and swims off again before the loop comes round. 181 of the 1000 cells ever change; on a typical quarter beat, 4 do. Under reduced motion it holds the frame where the coconut walks off.

Here is that frame with the colour switched off, in the C64's own start-up colours. Every cell is just a character:

<p align="center">
  <img src="assets/30-petscii-picture_opus_5.5-colour-off.svg" width="576" alt="The same PETSCII picture with its colours switched off: every character cell drawn in light blue on dark blue, like a Commodore 64 start-up screen. The sun, the clouds, the palm, the woman in headphones, the shrubs, the sandcastle, the crab under its coconut and the block letters of CASTAWAY are all visible as plain characters, the letters dark inside the light blue sea, with the caption THE COCONUT WALKS OFF. CRAB INSIDE.">
</p>

The 8 by 8 shapes are redrawn as plain bitmaps, not copied out of a ROM. Every cell of both pictures is placed by hand, in a small script that draws them.

</details>

<summary><b>Credits</b></summary>
<br>

```text
PICTURE ..................... HERMIT KERNING
SHOWN AT .................... TIDEMARK, AN ISLAND PARTY FOR ONE
PLACED ...................... 1ST OF 1, PETSCII COMPO
JUDGE ....................... THE CRAB (BUSY)
GRID ........................ 40 X 25
BACKGROUND COLOURS .......... 1
COLOURS IN THE PICTURE ...... 11 OF 16
BLACK ....................... 0 CELLS
CELLS THAT EVER CHANGE ...... 181
TURTLES ..................... 1 (ASLEEP)
COCONUTS LOST ............... 1, TO A CRAB
```

Thanks to the tide, which did all the foam, to the crab, who did not ask to be in this, and to the turtle, who slept through the credits.

</details>

A bottle comes back. A drone delivers more headphones. A coconut falls. It walks off with a crab inside. 90+ activities. 4 timers. Each one starts on the bar. Every sound is code. No samples. 80 BPM. F major. No seams. python tools/serve.py, open 127.0.0.1:8765 and wait, calmly. Supplied by the tide. Returned by the tide. Always daytime.">
</p>

Typical is the median of 200 simulated runs, as the file's own header puts it. Together that is about 200 timer events a run, with about 20 chained follow-ups on top. <details>
<summary><b>ABOUT THIS INTRO</b>: how the banner is made</summary>

<br>

The banner borrows the layout of a framed Amiga intro from around 1990-91: on black, a short grey strip holding a small logo plate, then a tall navy panel where the text itself carries the colour, three lines of wide slanted capitals filled with one rainbow. Its text page is the other half of the style: dense 8-pixel capitals in blocks tinted magenta, white, orange and light blue. Where those pages once said who supplied the release, this one says the tide did. The two windows in the grey strip are this banner's own addition.

- **Rainbow lines.** Each capital is drawn from a stroke skeleton with an elliptical pen, so the letters come out round, then slanted a pixel every four rows. All of them share one hard-stepped gradient across the panel, 48 twelve-bit colours, which moves one step every quarter second: colour cycling.
- **Pages.** Eight pages of three lines, two bars each (6 seconds at 80 BPM), 48 seconds a loop. Letters bob one pixel at a time on a wave that takes a bar, and fold away and back left to right when the page changes. Page one is in place on the first frame.
- **The plate.** A capsule with a three-pixel chrome rim, red capitals shaded row by row with white top edges, and a glint every two bars.
- **The windows.** Two 16:9 pictures, 39 by 22 pixels. She and the shark nod on every beat.
- **Calm.** Nothing large flashes: the colour cycle moves one neighbouring hue at a time, the letters move one pixel at a time, and the stars blink on the beat. With reduced motion switched on, everything holds on page one with the rainbow still.

No group's logo, letterforms or text were copied: the two fonts, the plate lettering and the sprites were drawn for this banner, and the words were written for it. The Palm Readers are invented. Rebuild both images with `node src/31-amiga-logo-plate-intro_opus_5.5.mjs`.

</details>

<br>

<h1 align="center">Castaway <sub><i>(working title)</i></sub></h1>

<p align="center">
  <b>A ten-hour lo-fi island video in which almost nothing happens, on purpose.</b><br>
  One young woman, one tall palm, one raft and a lot of time. She idles, nodding to the music on her headphones.<br>
  Every so often, something happens. Then she goes back to nodding.
</p>

<p align="center">
  <b>90+ activities</b> &nbsp;·&nbsp; <b>four timers</b> &nbsp;·&nbsp; <b>every gag on the beat</b> &nbsp;·&nbsp; <b>every sound synthesized from code</b> &nbsp;·&nbsp; <b>always daytime</b>
</p>

Castaway is a stationary-frame video for YouTube, in the spirit of the ten-hour lofi streams. Most of the time she just sits there. Then a message in a bottle washes straight back, or a shark in headphones nods along to the beat, or a coconut lands on a hermit crab and walks off with the crab wearing it. It is an unofficial remake inspired by the small-island routines and visual comedy of *Johnny Castaway*, the 1992 desert-island screensaver, repainted as a sunny, hand-painted coastal anime scene: 16:9, 1080p, 30 fps.

The gags live in [activities.toml](activities.toml), on four timers from every 2 to 5 minutes up to every 3 to 6 hours, and each one waits for the next bar of the music (every 3 seconds) so the punchlines land on the beat. Every sound is synthesized from code by [tools/make_audio.py](tools/make_audio.py): no samples, no loops, no recordings.

```sh
python tools/serve.py
```

Then open **http://127.0.0.1:8765/** for the live preview, and export a YouTube-ready MP4 from the same page. Plain ES modules, no build step, no npm. In development: no video has been published yet, so for now the only way to watch her wait is to run it.

<details>
<summary><b>WHAT IS ON THE SCREEN</b>: an inventory, taken over ten hours</summary>

```text
       . o O @ @ O o .     DRIFTWOOD BLITTER CO.     . o O @ @ O o .
             INVENTORY OF ONE VERY SMALL ISLAND, IN TWO PARTS
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 PART ONE: THE BANNER
   bobs ............................. 30, shaded blue, on a figure of eight
     of which coconuts .................................................. 1
   dots .................................. 406, arranged as a palm, turning
   women .......................................... 1, on the axis, nodding
   times she has looked up at the bobs .................................. 0
   crabs ...................................... 0, then 1 for 12 s a minute
   things the crab is wearing ................................... a coconut

 PART TWO: THE VIDEO
   palms ................................................................ 1
   rafts ................................................................ 1
   activities ......................................... more than 90 so far
   length of a run .................................... 10:00:00, seed 1992
   time spent busy .................................... about a third of it
   time spent idling ...................................... all of the rest
   night scenes ......................................................... 0
   samples, loops or recordings ......................................... 0
   people who have heard the soundtrack yet ............................. 0
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

**How the banner works.** It is two early Amiga intro effects from 1989 and 1990 at once: the chain of "bobs" (blitter-drawn balls) snaking round a figure of eight, and the "dot object", a shape made of single dots turning in space. Here the dot object is the island and the bobs orbit it. From the front the orbit is a figure of eight: across is one sine of the lap, height is another at a little over twice the speed, so once a minute the eight drifts through a smile, a frown and back. Every ball exists twice, once behind the island and once in front, and each copy only shows on its own half of the lap, so the chain passes behind the palm and then in front of it. The 30 balls are a tenth of a bar apart, so the chain fills three quarters of the lap and a single frame shows most of the eight. The balls swap between six pre-drawn sizes and move in whole Amiga pixels; the dots turn smoothly, dimming as they go round the back. One lap is 12 seconds, which is four bars of the theme, and she nods at 80 BPM. No script, no GIF, and with reduced motion switched on everything holds still on a full frame.

She sits exactly on the axis, which is why she never has to turn: the island turns under her. It is also, more or less, what she does in the video.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>THE TIMETABLE</b>: four timers, more than 90 activities, one bar at a time</summary>

| Timer | Comes round | In a typical 10-hour run | Some of what it can pick |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Regular | every 2 to 5 min | about 155 | a coconut sip, a stroll, jogging laps, fishing, a sandcastle |
| Occasional | every 12 to 25 min | about 30 | a ship passing unseen, a message in a bottle, a sea turtle, the coconut and the hermit crab, planting a kumara |
| Rare | every 30 to 60 min | about 13 | the delivery drone, the signal hunt, the cat on a crate, the shark in headphones, the tour boat, the hydrofoil bro, fire by friction, spear fishing, a hammock, a lookout up the palm |
| Super rare | every 3 to 6 hours, 3 a run at most | about 2 | she could leave any time |
| Chained | never on a timer, only after another gag | about 20 | the tide takes the sandcastle, a different bottle brings a reply, the kumara grows |

The counts are the median of 200 simulated runs, as the header of [activities.toml](activities.toml) says, and she is busy about a third of the time. When a timer goes off it picks one gag from its tier by weight, among those free to run. Lanes let things overlap: she has one lane, and the cat, the turtle, the sea and sky, and the shore each have their own, which is how a ship gets to sail past exactly while she is busy with a coconut. The default run is 10:00:00 with seed 1992. `python tools/schedule.py` checks the file and simulates one.

**A few of the gags, in full.** The bottle washes straight back; a different one turns up later with a reply. The drone's parcel is another pair of headphones. The grey tabby with the white chest arrives on a crate, climbs the palm, naps, and one day floats away again (another day it comes back). The signal hunt finds one bar, at the very top of the palm. The bro on the electric hydrofoil throws a shaka and carves off. And she could leave any time: she walks out over the water and comes back with an iced coffee.

**Scene life.** 26 entries: 4 always-on effects and 22 timed events. Shore waves and drifting cloud shadows are built; distant birds, planes with vapour trails, whale pods, dolphins, sailboats, sandpipers, a gecko and a rain shower are planned. Daytime rain, naturally.

</details>

- **Sound.** Everything is synthesized from code by [tools/make_audio.py](tools/make_audio.py): more than 150 sound files and no samples, stock loops or recordings, so no third-party licence applies. The theme is a seamless 60-second loop at 80 BPM in F major (ii-V-I-vi), 20 bars of exactly 3 seconds, on electric piano, a kalimba lead, soft drums and vinyl crackle; the ocean ambience is a seamless 60-second loop too. The mix sits at -14 LUFS with true peak at or below -1 dBTP, and levels are adjustable in master and per routine. It has been measured with great care. Nobody has listened to it yet.
- **Renderer.** A web page ([web/index.html](web/index.html)) served by [tools/serve.py](tools/serve.py), with live preview and export: the browser encodes frame-exact H.264 with WebCodecs (68 to 78 frames a second at 1080p30 in Chrome) and the server mixes in the sound and joins the two into an MP4. Hard cuts and stepped movement are the motion defaults.
- **Tools.** `python tools/schedule.py` validates the schedule and simulates a ten-hour run. `python tools/render_demo.py --dev` renders a dev reel of every activity with a heads-up display, from the older Python reference renderer ([tools/render_demo.py](tools/render_demo.py)).
- **Status.** In development. No video, no public link yet. The working log is [MUSING.md](MUSING.md).

<h3 align="center">CASTAWAY <sub><i>(working title)</i></sub></h3>

<p align="center">
  <b>A ten-hour lo-fi island video, written in two instructions: WAIT and MOVE.</b><br>
  She mostly waits. Every so often, something moves.
</p>

<p align="center">
  <kbd>WAIT</kbd> for the next bar (3&nbsp;s)
  &nbsp;·&nbsp;
  <kbd>MOVE</kbd> one gag, on the beat
  &nbsp;·&nbsp;
  <kbd>$FFFF,$FFFE</kbd> the end of every copper list
</p>

A stationary-frame lo-fi video for YouTube, in the spirit of the ten-hour lofi streams: a young woman alone on a tiny island with one tall palm, a raft and a lot of time. She mostly idles, nodding to the music on her headphones, and every so often something happens. A message in a bottle washes straight back. A shark in headphones nods to the beat. A coconut falls on a hermit crab, and the coconut walks off with the crab wearing it. It is an unofficial remake inspired by the small-island routines and visual comedy of *Johnny Castaway*, the 1992 desert-island screensaver, repainted as a sunny, hand-painted coastal anime scene. 16:9 at 1080p, and always daytime.

More than 90 activities live in [activities.toml](activities.toml), on four timers: regular every 2 to 5 minutes, occasional every 12 to 25, rare every 30 to 60, super rare every 3 to 6 hours. Each one waits for the next bar of the music before it starts, so the gags land on the beat, and lanes let two things happen at once. Every sound is synthesized from code by [tools/make_audio.py](tools/make_audio.py): no samples, no loops, no recordings, so no third-party licence. Nobody has heard it yet. A meter has, and reports -14 LUFS.

```sh
python tools/serve.py
# then open http://127.0.0.1:8765/
```

The page previews the island live and exports a YouTube-ready MP4: the browser encodes frame-exact H.264 with WebCodecs, and the server mixes in the sound. Plain ES modules, no build step, no npm packages. Still in development: no video is published and there is no link. To watch her wait, run it.

<details>
<summary><b>THE COPPER LIST</b>: the island in two words, and her day in the same two words</summary>

On an Amiga, the copper is a tiny co-processor with three instructions, and a copper screen gets by on two of them. WAIT until the video beam reaches a given spot on the screen. MOVE a value into a register, such as the background colour. A copper-only screen is a picture made of nothing else: no bitmap, no pixels behind it, just a very long list of colour changes timed to the beam. This is the island in the banner, written that way.

```text
 ; ISLAND.COP: one island, no bitplanes. COLOR00 is the background colour.
 ; WAIT for the beam to reach a line, then MOVE a 12-bit colour ($0RGB).
 ; (Illustrative. The banner is an SVG, and this was never run on a 500.)

 island:  dc.w $2c01,$fffe,$0180,$038c   ; WAIT line 44     MOVE sky, deep
          dc.w $3201,$fffe,$0180,$07be   ; WAIT line 50     MOVE sky, paler
          dc.w $3b01,$fffe,$0180,$0cef   ; WAIT line 59     MOVE haze
          dc.w $3c01,$fffe,$0180,$0dff   ; WAIT line 60     MOVE horizon
          dc.w $3d01,$fffe,$0180,$05df   ; WAIT line 61     MOVE sea, crest
          dc.w $3e01,$fffe,$0180,$0059   ; WAIT line 62     MOVE sea, trough
          ;  ...one or two MOVEs a line, all the way down the sea...
          dc.w $4b61,$fffe,$0180,$0fe9   ; WAIT line 75, mid-line: sand
          dc.w $4ba1,$fffe,$0180,$0059   ; WAIT further along: sea again
          ;  ...and the sand gets four pixels wider every other line...
          dc.w $ffff,$fffe               ; WAIT for a spot the beam never hits
```

That last line is how every copper list ends: wait for a beam position the screen never reaches, and sit there until the next frame. It is also, roughly, the plot.

```text
 ; HERDAY.COP: the same two instructions, ten hours long.

 day:     WAIT  next bar                 ; every activity starts on a bar line
          MOVE  idle, nodding            ; about two thirds of the time
          WAIT  2 to 5 minutes           ; regular
          MOVE  coconut, fishing, a jog  ; about 155 of these in ten hours
          WAIT  12 to 25 minutes         ; occasional
          MOVE  bottle: thrown, returned
          WAIT  30 to 60 minutes         ; rare
          MOVE  shark in headphones, nodding to the beat
          WAIT  3 to 6 hours             ; super rare, 3 a run at most
          MOVE  she walks out over the water; back with an iced coffee
          WAIT  $ffff,$fffe              ; she could leave any time
```

**The maths.** At 80 BPM a bar is 3 seconds, so a ten-hour video has 12,000 bar lines. In a typical run (the median of 200 simulated runs) about 200 of them start something, plus the chained follow-ups those set off. The other 11,800 or so are a WAIT. She is busy about a third of the time and perfectly content the rest of it.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>THE WINDOWS</b>: what each one shows, and how the banner works</summary>

Copper-only screens were a 1990 Amiga party trick. Colour can change on every scanline but only every few pixels along one, so everything on them is wide and short, and each effect sat in its own window with a thin light frame. This banner keeps both rules.

- **The top window** is soft diagonal bands in four 16-step ramps: palm green, sand, sea and foam. It is 39 columns, each 8 pixels wide and filled with one 64-colour hard-stop gradient, each column 4 scanlines out of step with the last. That offset is the whole diagonal. The lot rolls down one scanline per step: 128 steps in 12 seconds, which is four bars of the theme.
- **SUN** is a diamond of nested colour, blue core to red edge, pulsing outward. A copper changes colour only every 8 pixels along a line, so circles come out lumpy and the sun is a diamond. It does not seem to mind. Every cell gets a level (four per 8-pixel column, one per line from the centre), cells of one level share a class, and all 32 classes cycle the same palette, each one step behind the last: palette cycling, with no script.
- **ISLAND** is one colour per line for the sky, a sea of cyan lines whose phase is one over the distance from the horizon (so the crests come in and spread out), sand whose edges only move in four-pixel steps, foam that flips on every beat, a raft that bobs once a bar, and a palm whose trunk is the classic twisted ribbon: one bar per line, in red-tan and grey stripes, swayed and twisted by two shared keyframe tracks.
- **LANES** is red, green and blue bars sliding across each other. Where they cross, red and green make yellow, green and blue make cyan, red and blue make magenta. In [activities.toml](activities.toml), lanes are what let two things happen at once: her lane, the sea and sky, the shore, the cat, the turtle and the kumara patch. This is what that looks like to a copper.

**The sprites.** The title is eight hardware sprites, one letter each. The Amiga has exactly eight sprites and CASTAWAY has exactly eight letters, which is the closest this project has come to fate. Each one is 16 pixels wide and three colours, recoloured on every line. She is two attached sprites (15 colours), reused further down the screen once the title has finished with them, and she nods once per beat. Sprites are not bitplanes, so she counts. The small text is where the banner bends the rules.

**Timing.** Everything loops on bar lines of the 80 BPM theme: her nod every 0.75 seconds, the WAIT WAIT WAIT MOVE bar and the sea every 3, the sun and the plaid every 6, the bands every 12. No GIF, no script, no filters. With reduced motion switched on, every window holds still on a complete frame.

The style is credited to *Copper Master* by Angels and *Look! No bitplanes* by Razor 1911, both from October 1990, as the reference. Nothing of theirs is reused: the windows, palettes, letters, sprite and words were all drawn from scratch by the generator.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>THE REST OF THE LIST</b>: gags, scene life, tools, the theme and the greetz</summary>

**Some of what eventually MOVEs**

- A ship crosses the horizon while she is busy. It waits until she is busy, then it goes.
- A message in a bottle washes straight back. Much later, a different bottle brings a reply.
- A delivery drone lowers a parcel. It is another pair of headphones.
- A sea turtle visits. A shark in headphones nods to the beat.
- A grey tabby with a white chest arrives on a crate, climbs the palm and naps. One day it floats away again. Another day it comes back.
- The signal hunt: one bar of signal, at the very top of the palm.
- A tour boat of selfie-takers. A bro on an electric hydrofoil throws a shaka and carves off.
- Bushcraft: fire by friction, a hammock, a lookout up the palm, spear fishing. A kumara she plants grows over the course of the video.
- Coconut sipping, fishing, jogging laps, waving for rescue, and a sandcastle the tide takes.

**Scene life.** 26 entries. Built: shore waves and drifting cloud shadows. Planned: distant birds, planes with vapour trails, whale pods, dolphins, sailboats, sandpipers, a gecko and a rain shower (in daylight, like everything else).

```text
 ; TOOLS.COP
          python tools/serve.py          ; the renderer: live preview, MP4
          python tools/schedule.py       ; validate, simulate ten hours
          python tools/make_audio.py     ; synthesize every sound from code
          python tools/render_demo.py --dev
                                         ; a dev reel of every activity
 ; THEME.COP
          ; 60 s seamless loop, 80 BPM, F major, ii-V-I-vi, 20 bars of 3 s
          ; electric piano, kalimba lead, soft drums, vinyl crackle
          ; mix at -14 LUFS, true peak at or below -1 dBTP; levels adjust
          ; in master and per routine. The ocean is a 60 s loop as well.
          ; Default run: 10:00:00, seed 1992.
```

**Greetz** to the Display List Society, the Palette Cycling Club (Tuesdays, weather permitting), the Colour Clock Repair Shop, the Raster Bar Bathers and the Seagull Union, whose calls have been synthesized without their consent.

**No greetz** to the beam, which has never once reached the end of a copper list.

**Small print.** Castaway is an unofficial project inspired by *Johnny Castaway* (1992), which belongs to its owners; nothing from it is used in this header. Mid-Line Movers and everyone in the greetz are made up.

## 34 · Moire Silhouette

<sub><code>34-moire-silhouette_opus_5.5.md</code></sub>

<p align="center">
  <img src="assets/34-moire-silhouette_opus_5.5.svg" width="100%" alt="CASTAWAY, as an early-90s Amiga rave-demo screen. Two sets of broad concentric rings, one centred behind the crown of a palm tree and one a little lower and to the right, overlap into a moire of crescents and swirls in clashing green, crimson and violet, and both centres drift slowly so the pattern crawls. Cut out of the same rings in yellow and orange, with no outline, stands one big silhouette: a small island with a tall curving palm, fronds spread wide like arms, a raft with a rag flag moored on the left, and a young woman in headphones sitting cross-legged on the sand, nodding on every beat. The palm dances on the beat too: lean left, reach up, lean right, dip. A hermit crab shuffles in under the coconuts, one drops on it, bonk, and the coconut gets up and walks off down the beach and into the sea with the crab wearing it. Then she stands and waves for rescue with both arms up, and the palm does the same move, much bigger. Once a bar, every three seconds, the colours cut to a new pair: sun, sea, coral, palm. Along the bottom, on a flat dark band, CASTAWAY in plain heavy capitals, with 10:00:00 on the left and 80 BPM on the right.">
</p>

<h1 align="center">CASTAWAY <sub><i>(working title)</i></sub></h1>

<p align="center">
  <b>A ten-hour all-dayer for one woman, one palm and, eventually, one crab in a coconut.</b><br>
  She nods to the music. Every so often, something happens. The palm, it turns out, has been dancing the whole time.
</p>

<p align="center">
  <kbd>ALL-DAYER</kbd> 10:00:00, strictly no night
  &nbsp;·&nbsp;
  <kbd>80 BPM</kbd> every gag waits for the next bar
  &nbsp;·&nbsp;
  <kbd>CAPACITY</kbd> 1 (and a cat, some days)
</p>

**Castaway** is a stationary-frame lo-fi video for YouTube, in the spirit of the ten-hour lofi streams: a young woman alone on a tiny island with one tall palm, a raft and a lot of time. She mostly idles, nodding to the music on her headphones, and every so often something happens. It is an unofficial remake, inspired by the small-island routines and visual comedy of *Johnny Castaway*, the 1992 desert-island screensaver, repainted as a sunny, hand-painted coastal anime scene. 16:9, 1080p, 30 fps, always daytime.

The line-up is [activities.toml](activities.toml): more than 90 activities, most of them on four timers, from every 2 to 5 minutes (a coconut, a lap, some fishing) up to every 3 to 6 hours (the super-rare ones: about two a video, so don't blink). A message in a bottle washes straight back. A shark in headphones nods along. A coconut lands on a hermit crab, and the crab leaves wearing it. Every activity starts on the next bar of the music (every 3 seconds), so the gags land on the beat. In a typical ten-hour run she is busy about a third of the time and idle for the rest, which is the point.

Every sound is synthesized from code by [tools/make_audio.py](tools/make_audio.py): no samples, no loops, no recordings, so no third-party licence applies. More than 150 sound files so far, all measured, none yet heard by a human.

```sh
python tools/serve.py
# then open http://127.0.0.1:8765/
```

Live preview in the page, then export a YouTube-ready MP4: the browser encodes frame-exact H.264 with WebCodecs and the server mixes in the sound. Plain ES modules, no build step, no npm. [tools/schedule.py](tools/schedule.py) checks the schedule and simulates ten hours of it. In development: no video has been published yet, so for now the only way to watch her wait is to run it.

<details>
<summary><b>THE DANCE CARD</b>: what the banner does for 24 seconds, beat by beat, and how</summary>

```text
  THE DANCE CARD · 8 BARS · 24 SECONDS · THEN AGAIN, FOR TEN HOURS
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  BAR  COLOURS  THE PALM                     HER        THE CRAB
  1    sun      lean · reach · lean · dip    nod x4     shuffles in
  2    sea      lean · reach · lean · dip    nod x4     under the coconuts
  3    coral    lean · reach · lean · dip    nod x4     coconut. bonk.
  4    palm     lean · reach · lean · dip    nod x4     gets up, wearing it
  5    sun      lean · reach · lean · dip    nod x4     through the bushes
  6    sea      lean · reach · lean · dip    nod x4     down the beach, gone
  7    coral    both arms up                 up, waving for rescue
  8    palm     both arms up                 still waving. nobody comes.
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  One pose per beat at 80 BPM, the same hard cuts the project uses for
  her own frames. The palm has never been told it is not the main act.
```

**How the banner works.** Each set of rings is a single rectangle filled with a repeating radial gradient with hard stops. One set is used as a mask; the other is drawn once everywhere and once more inside the mask with its colours swapped, which composites to an XOR of the two: that is the moire, with no blend modes and no filters. Outside the figure the four ring cases map to three colours; inside, the same two ring sets map to two other colours, clipped by the silhouette, so the island, the palm and she read only by the change of colour. Both centres drift on slow ellipses that close every 24 seconds, so the swirls crawl and the rings never jump at the loop point; only the story cuts back to the start, on the beat, like everything else.

The palm's six poses, her four, the crab, the falling coconut and the walking coconut are paths in one clip, each with a stepped visibility track, and everything cuts on the beat. The colours cut once a bar, which keeps the whole thing far below three changes a second. With reduced motion switched on, it holds still on one complete frame: palm, rings, her and the crab, all in place.

The look is modelled on the early-90s Amiga rave demos that cut one traced dancer out of moire rings, above all Spaceballs' *State of the Art* (1992), credited here as the reference. No dancer, frame or name of theirs is used: the palm, the island, her, the crab and the letters were all drawn from scratch by the generator.

</details>

<p align="center"><sub>Castaway is an unofficial project inspired by <i>Johnny Castaway</i> (1992), which belongs to its owners; nothing from it is used here. Two Centres and everyone in the big-ups are made up. Strictly no night: it is a project rule.</sub></p>

<h1 align="center">Castaway</h1>

<p align="center">
  <b>Ten hours on one tiny island. Almost nothing happens, polished to a high shine.</b><br>
  <sub>A demo logo is the thing you stare at while you wait. Castaway is ten hours of waiting, so it got a proper one.</sub>
</p>

Castaway (working title) is a stationary-frame lo-fi video for YouTube, in the spirit of the ten-hour lofi streams: a young woman alone on a tiny island with one tall palm, a raft and a lot of time. She mostly idles, nodding to the music on her headphones, and every so often something happens. A message in a bottle washes up and goes straight back out. A delivery drone drops off a parcel, and the parcel is another pair of headphones. A coconut falls on a hermit crab, and then the coconut walks off, because the crab is wearing it. It is an unofficial remake, inspired by the small-island routines and visual comedy of *Johnny Castaway*, the 1992 desert-island screensaver, repainted as a sunny, hand-painted coastal anime scene: 16:9, 1080p, 30 fps, and always daytime.

**The schedule.** More than 90 activities live in [activities.toml](activities.toml). Most run on four timers: everyday routines every 2 to 5 minutes, small gags every 12 to 25, set pieces every 30 to 60, and super-rare callbacks every 3 to 6 hours. The rest are follow-ups that wait for their cue. Each one waits for the next bar of the music (3 seconds) before it starts, so the gags land on the beat. The glint on the logo above keeps the same rule, then sits out the next three bars, which is very much the house style.

**The sound.** Every sound is synthesized from code by [tools/make_audio.py](tools/make_audio.py): no samples, no loops, no recordings, so no third-party licence applies. The theme is a seamless 60-second loop at 80 BPM.

```sh
python tools/serve.py
# then open http://127.0.0.1:8765/
```

<p align="center">
  <sub>Live preview in the browser, then export a frame-exact, YouTube-ready MP4. Plain ES modules, no build step, no npm packages.<br>
  In development: no video has been published yet. For now the island only takes visitors on port 8765.</sub>
</p>

<details>
<summary><b>ONE LETTER, UP CLOSE</b>: how the logo is put together, pixel by pixel</summary>
<br>

<p align="center">
  <img src="assets/35-hand-pixelled-chrome-logo_opus_5.5-magnify.svg" width="100%" alt="The W from the Castaway logo on its own, magnified three times on a black panel with the pixel grid drawn over it, and notes on the right with leader lines to the pixels they describe: lit top edge, a white row; sky, violet to pale blue; one-pixel black outline; bands meet, checkerboard; horizon, glare and zigzag; an island in the chrome, a tiny dark palm on a mound in the W's left stem; extruded 5 px down-right; sand, dark to light. Underneath, the banner's palette in 32 slots: 29 swatches filled, from black and violets through white, reds, oranges and sand, sea blues, three cat greys and a pink, and 3 empty slots. Label: the banner's palette, 32 slots, 29 used, all 12-bit.">
</p>

**The recipe.** Between 1988 and 1993 an Amiga or Atari ST group logo was drawn dot by dot in a paint program, 320 pixels wide and in 16 or 32 colours, and chrome was a favourite finish: metal capitals reflecting an imaginary sky above a hard horizon and an imaginary desert below it, banded because the palette is tiny. This one keeps the recipe and moves the desert to the seaside. Sky from violet to pale blue, a white line of glare along a horizon that zigzags like small waves, coral and sand underneath, a one-pixel black outline, a lit top edge, a side extruded five pixels down and to the right, and white stars on the corners.

**The honest version of "hand-pixelled".** No paint program was involved. A Node script builds the capitals from chamfered rectangles, leans them one pixel every three rows, picks every pixel of a 320 by 140 buffer itself (bands, bevels, outlines, dither and all), then writes the pixels out colour by colour as merged SVG paths. Every colour is a 12-bit Amiga value, one hex digit a channel, and the script refuses to build if the banner needs more than 32 of them. It needs 29. Like the island: plenty of room, not much going on, on purpose.

**The island in the W.** Chrome reflects whatever world the artist imagines, and this one imagined a palm. Look at the W's left stem, just above the horizon. She is not on that island. She is busy.

**The cat** is the grey tabby from the stray-cat gag, which in the video arrives on a crate, climbs the palm and naps. Here it has found the T, which is flatter. It is not part of the logo, and nobody has had the heart to tell it.

```text
 THE LOGO'S TIMETABLE · 80 BPM · ONE BEAT 0.75 s · ONE BAR 3 s
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  stars ............ one twinkle per bar each, a beat apart
  sea .............. ripples sideways once a beat; sun glints too
  cat .............. tail flicks every 2 beats; one z every 2 beats
  glint ............ sets off on the first beat of every fourth bar,
                     takes three beats to cross, then waits
  subtitle ......... a new line every 2 bars, hard cuts
  whole picture .... one 36-second loop, no seams
  reduced motion ... holds still: big stars, no glint, line one
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  the video's motion defaults are hard cuts and stepped movement.
  the logo agreed to the same terms
```

The style is credited to the Amiga and Atari ST logo artists of 1988 to 1993: the Red Sector Megademo title (violet top, zigzag horizon, orange-red base), the blue-to-white-to-grey menu logo of Kefrens' Megademo 8, and the red and blue logos in Phenomena's Enigma, which Demozoo credits to Uno. Nothing of theirs is copied: no letterforms, no palette, no logos, and none of their names on the banner. The capitals, the colours, the small font and the cat were made for this banner.

</details>

## 36 · Atari ST Menu Disk

<sub><code>36-st-menu-disk_opus_5.5.md</code></sub>

<p align="center">
